promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: The social construction of crime and deviance

questions.q: Which of the following is the best definition of deviance?
options: Behaviour that breaks the formal laws of a country
Behaviour that breaks the norms and values of a society
Behaviour that is always punished by the police
Behaviour that is approved of by the majority
questions.explain: Deviance is any behaviour that goes against the accepted norms and values of a society, whether or not it is illegal.

questions.q: Which statement best defines crime?
options: Any behaviour that offends other people
Behaviour that breaks the law of a society
Behaviour that is considered immoral by religion
Any act that is unusual or rare
questions.explain: A crime is an act that breaks the formal written laws of a society and can be punished by the state.

questions.q: Sociologists argue that crime and deviance are 'socially constructed'. This means that
options: Everyone in the world agrees on what is deviant
What counts as deviant varies between different times, places and cultures
Deviance is caused only by an individual's biology
Deviant acts are fixed and never change
questions.explain: Because definitions of deviance differ by society, time and situation, deviance is seen as socially constructed rather than fixed.

questions.q: A reward given to encourage approved behaviour is best described as a
options: Negative sanction
Positive sanction
Formal law
Master status
questions.explain: A positive sanction is a reward, such as praise or a prize, used to encourage conformity to norms.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of an informal negative sanction?
options: Being sent to prison by a judge
Being fined by a court
Being given a disapproving look by a parent
Being expelled from school by the head teacher
questions.explain: Informal negative sanctions are unofficial responses such as disapproval, gossip or ridicule from people around us.

questions.q: According to Durkheim, a functionalist, crime is
options: Entirely harmful and serves no purpose
Inevitable in society and can perform useful functions
Caused only by capitalism
The result of a criminal gene
questions.explain: Durkheim argued crime is inevitable and can be functional, for example by reinforcing shared values and marking the boundaries of acceptable behaviour.

questions.q: Merton's strain theory explains crime as resulting from
options: A gap between society's goals and the legitimate means to achieve them
Faulty labelling by the police
The influence of a criminal peer group only
Inherited biological traits
questions.explain: Merton argued that when people cannot reach socially valued goals such as wealth by legitimate means, this strain (anomie) can push some towards crime.

questions.q: In labelling theory, Becker argued that deviance is best understood as
options: A quality found in the act itself
Something created by society's reaction to certain behaviour
Always caused by poverty
A natural instinct in all humans
questions.explain: Becker claimed no act is inherently deviant; deviance is created when others label and react to the behaviour and the person.

questions.q: Albert Cohen's subcultural theory links delinquency among some working-class boys to
options: Status frustration and the search for status in a delinquent subculture
A lack of formal social control agencies
The chivalry of the police
An accurate reading of official statistics
questions.explain: Cohen argued boys who fail to gain status at school may experience status frustration and gain status instead within a delinquent subculture.

questions.q: A teenager is caught shoplifting once, is publicly labelled a 'criminal', and afterwards commits further crimes as he is treated as an outsider. Which theory best explains this?
options: Functionalist theory
Labelling theory
Biological theory
Chivalry thesis
questions.explain: This illustrates labelling theory, where a deviant label becomes a master status that can lead to a self-fulfilling prophecy and further deviance.

questions.q: Marxist sociologists tend to argue that the law and criminal justice system
options: Treat all social classes equally
Mainly serve the interests of the powerful ruling class
Are unnecessary in modern society
Are shaped only by individual choice
questions.explain: Marxists argue laws are made and enforced in ways that protect the interests of the wealthy and powerful rather than being neutral.

questions.q: Which of the following is an agency of formal social control?
options: The family
The peer group
The police
Friends
questions.explain: Formal social control is carried out by official agencies such as the police, courts and prisons that enforce written rules and laws.

questions.q: Which statement best describes informal social control?
options: It is enforced by courts using official punishments
It works through unwritten rules and agencies such as the family and peer group
It only exists in modern industrial societies
It relies entirely on imprisonment
questions.explain: Informal social control operates through everyday agencies like the family, peers, religion and the media using unofficial sanctions.

questions.q: Which of the following is an agency of informal social control?
options: The prison service
The family
The court system
The armed forces
questions.explain: The family is a key agency of informal social control, teaching norms and values through primary socialisation.

questions.q: A group of friends stops speaking to a member who lies to them until she apologises. This is an example of
options: Formal social control by the state
Informal social control through the peer group
A positive sanction
The dark figure of crime
questions.explain: Withdrawing friendship until behaviour changes is an informal negative sanction used by the peer group to enforce conformity.

questions.q: The 'dark figure of crime' refers to
options: Crimes committed at night
Crime that is unreported and/or unrecorded and so missing from official statistics
Crimes committed by powerful people
The total number of prisoners
questions.explain: The dark figure of crime is the hidden amount of crime that never appears in official statistics because it is not reported or recorded.

questions.q: A victim survey measures crime by
options: Counting only crimes recorded by the police
Asking people whether they have been victims of crime, including unreported offences
Asking offenders to list crimes they have committed
Counting the number of people in prison
questions.explain: Victim surveys ask a sample of people about crimes committed against them, helping to reveal crime not shown in police records.

questions.q: A self-report study collects information about crime by
options: Asking people to admit anonymously to crimes they have committed
Reading court records
Interviewing police officers
Counting recorded crimes
questions.explain: Self-report studies ask respondents to reveal crimes they have committed, often anonymously, uncovering offences not recorded officially.

questions.q: Which of the following is a common reason why a crime might NOT be reported to the police?
options: The victim thinks the crime is too trivial or that the police can do nothing
The crime automatically appears in official statistics
All crimes are always reported by law
Reporting crime is impossible
questions.explain: People often fail to report crime because they see it as trivial, fear reprisals, distrust the police or feel nothing can be done.

questions.q: Official statistics show far more crime is committed by young males than by older females. A sociologist warns these figures may be unreliable because
options: Statistics record every crime that is committed
Some groups may be more likely to be labelled, stopped or reported, so statistics may not reflect the true pattern
Young males never commit crime
Victim surveys are always inaccurate
questions.explain: Official statistics can reflect the reactions of agencies such as the police rather than the true amount and distribution of crime.

specSource: Cambridge IGCSE Sociology (0495) syllabus; Crime, Deviance & Social Control
